# Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization

Zishun Yu Affiliation: MetaAI Affiliation: The University of Illinois
Chicago Work done at Meta    Tengyu Xu Affiliation: MetaAI    Di Jin
Affiliation: MetaAI    Karthik Abinav Sankararaman Affiliation: MetaAI
   Yun He Affiliation: MetaAI    Wenxuan Zhou Affiliation: MetaAI   
Zhouhao Zeng Affiliation: MetaAI    Eryk Helenowski Affiliation: MetaAI
   Chen Zhu Affiliation: MetaAI    Sinong Wang Affiliation: MetaAI   
Hao Ma Affiliation: MetaAI    Han Fang Affiliation: MetaAI

###### Abstract

Solving mathematics problems has been an intriguing capability of large
language models, and many efforts have been made to improve reasoning by
extending reasoning length, such as through self-correction and
extensive long chain-of-thoughts. While promising in problem-solving,
advanced long reasoning chain models exhibit an undesired single-modal
behavior, where trivial questions require unnecessarily tedious long
chains of thought. In this work, we propose a way to allow models to be
aware of inference budgets by formulating it as utility maximization
with respect to an inference budget constraint, hence naming our
algorithm Inference Budget-Constrained Policy Optimization (IBPO). In a
nutshell, models fine-tuned through IBPO learn to “understand” the
difficulty of queries and allocate inference budgets to harder ones.
With different inference budgets, our best models are able to have a
$`4.14`$% and $`5.74`$% absolute improvement ($`8.08`$% and $`11.2`$%
relative improvement) on MATH500 using $`2.16`$x and $`4.32`$x inference
budgets respectively, relative to LLaMA3.1 8B Instruct. These
improvements are approximately $`2`$x those of self-consistency under
the same budgets.

## 1 Introduction

Complex reasoning has been an intriguing ability of large language
models (LLMs), with application in for example mathematical
problem-solving ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib14); [Hendrycks et al.,
2021b](#bib.bib29); [Lightman et al., 2023](#bib.bib41)) or
coding ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib9); [Austin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib5); [Hendrycks et al., 2021a](#bib.bib28)), which does not
only require nature language comprehending but also logical and critical
“thinking”. An observation merged in the LLM reasoning literature is
that longer reasoning traces often leads to improved reasoning soundness
and correctness. The seminal work of chain-of-thought (CoT) ([Wei
et al., 2022](#bib.bib69)) is an excellent example of how enriching
reasoning details, by decomposing reasoning traces into steps, improves
its problem-solving capability. CoT has been considered a standard
technique in reasoning, recent works extend CoT by allow LLMs to expand
its reasoning steps, by for example CoT with more steps ([Jin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)) (as explicitly required by instruction),
self-reflection/correction ([Madaan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Zelikman
et al., 2022](#bib.bib76); [Yan et al., 2024](#bib.bib73); [Qu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)), multi-turn reasoning ([Kumar et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)) or multi-agent debate ([Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib40); [Pham et al., 2023](#bib.bib54)) (as a heterogeneous
case of multi-turn). It was conjectured that scaling the test-time
compute or the reasoning length unleashes LLMs’ potential for
reasoning ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)), which has been empirically
verified by recent hype of ultra-long reasoning models, such as
OpenAI-o1 ([Jaech et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)) and
DeepSeek-R1 ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)). We’ll later
categorizes these type of responses as (standard) CoT responses,
extended responses, and (ultra-)long responses, respectively, given the
nature of their reasoning lengths.

While scaling reasoning length is promising in problem-solving, advanced
long reasoning-chain models show an undesired uni-modal behavior that
trivial questions may require unnecessarily tedious long reasoning
trace, an example is shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
This uni-modal behavior creates unnecessarily higher inference costs and
increased carbon footprints ([Henderson et al., 2020](#bib.bib27);
[Anthony et al., 2020](#bib.bib4)). To partially address this, we study
how to enable multi-modal behavior for reasoning models in a way the
length of reasoning traces are automatically adjusted according to the
hardness level of the queries. From the aspect of query-adaptive
reasoning length, some heuristic methods ([Aggarwal et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Xu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib71); [Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib67), e.g.) have

![Refer to caption](2501.17974v2/figures/o1.jpg)

Figure 1: A long reasoning-chain model spent more than enough inference
time on a trivial problem.

been making effort towards better token efficiency, by which is meant
better accuracy with (hopefully) less token overhead. We take a
reinforcement learning (RL) perspective, where the accuracy gain over
the token overhead is nothing but a non-differentiable objective to be
optimized. One could, for instance, take the negative response length or
a metric of this sort as an intrinsic reward ([Chentanez et al.,
2004](#bib.bib12); [Pathak et al., 2017](#bib.bib51)). However,
balancing the intrinsic and extrinsic (accuracy) rewards might also be
challenging ([Liu et al., 2021](#bib.bib42)), and might be vulnerable to
reward hacking ([Pan et al., 2022](#bib.bib50); [Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib59); [Karwowski et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)).

Instead explicit modeling the length of responses, we take a more
abstract formulation, where we consider labeling each response $`y`$
with an unique group label
$`\mathcal{G}_{i}:i\in\llbracket G\rrbracket`$ for total number of $`G`$
groups, so that the union of these disjoint groups exactly form the
response space $`\cup_{i}\mathcal{G}_{i}=\mathcal{Y}`$. For example
$`\mathcal{G}`$ could be the group of CoT responses (with standard
length) or extended responses. We could then impose an density
constraint on each or a set of groups, by caping
$`\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(x)}[\mathbbm{1}_{\{y\in\mathcal{G}_{i}\}}]\leq q_{i}`$
for some prompt distribution $`\mu`$ and some response distribution
$`\pi(x)`$, induced from LLMs, conditioned on a prompt $`x`$. This
naturally formulates a constrained RL ([Garcıa and Fernández,
2015](#bib.bib22); [Altman, 2021](#bib.bib2)) problem. Also this group
definition is motivated by the resource-allocation literature ([Chenery
and Kretschmer, 1956](#bib.bib11); [Ibaraki and Katoh,
1988](#bib.bib31); [Karlin, 2003](#bib.bib35)), from the optimization
and econometric communities, which have been later applied in many
machine learning applications ([Zemel et al., 2013](#bib.bib77);
[Badanidiyuru et al., 2018](#bib.bib6), e.g.). This generalization
allows potential broader application of our algorithm as discussed in
Section [6](#S6 "6 Conclusion & Discussions ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
We’ve now set our goal of this work:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Therefore, one could control how responses of different lengths (which
are supposed to belong to different groups) are distributed. Our
rationale of algorithm design is given in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
derived from an optimization perspective but ended as a very simple
generalization of iterative supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods such as
reward-ranking fine-tuning (RAFT) ([Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) and
rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib49);
[Touvron et al., 2023](#bib.bib64)), see details in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
Given the motivation of our algorithm, we call the resulted algorithm as
Inference Budget-Constrained Policy Optimization (IBPO).

Paper structure. In
Section [2](#S2 "2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
we present the derivation of our algorithm from an optimization
perspective, resulting in a simple weighted iterative SFT update.
Section [3](#S3 "3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
provides further details on our practical implementation, including the
choice of the base algorithm and the design of reward.
Section [4](#S4 "4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
introduces the experimental settings used for empirical evaluation. The
final empirical results of our IBPO are presented in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
And
Section [6](#S6 "6 Conclusion & Discussions ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
concludes our work with limitations, broader impact, and further
discussions.

## 2 Algorithm Design

Problem setup. To make the notation compact, we take the sequence-level
notation (or the bandit notation), commonly used in LLMs ([Ziegler
et al., 2019](#bib.bib81); [Rafailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib56)),
especially in preference modeling, that suppresses the transition
probabilities and intermediate rewards, and see a response as a whole.
In particular, a policy $`\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y})`$ takes
a prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ and draw a response
$`a_{1}\circ a_{2}\dots\circ a_{T}=:y\in\mathcal{Y}`$ from the produced
probability simplex $`\Delta(\mathcal{Y})`$, where $`\circ`$ denotes
concatenation, $`a_{i}\in\mathcal{V}`$ corresponds to the $`i`$-th token
drawn from the vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$, and $`T`$ is the maximum
length. A LLM is a parametric policy
$`\pi_{\theta}\in\Pi_{\theta}\subseteq\Pi`$, where $`\Pi_{\theta}`$ and
$`\Pi`$ are the parametric and non-parametric policy space respectively.
Let $`\mathcal{J}(\pi;\mu,r)`$ or sometimes $`\mathcal{J}(\pi)`$ be a
general objective function, defined by a prompt distribution
$`\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal{X})`$, and a bounded reward function
$`r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-R_{\mathrm{max}},R_{\mathrm{max}}]`$.
Also, we define $`{\mu}_{\Omega}`$ as an empirical distribution induced
from $`\Omega`$, a set of prompts.

As aforementioned, we define $`G`$ disjoint groups $`\mathcal{G}_{i}`$
such that $`\cup_{i}\mathcal{G}_{i}=\mathcal{Y}`$ and
$`\mathcal{G}_{i}\cap\mathcal{G}_{j}=\emptyset`$ for all $`i\neq j`$.
Each response $`y\in\mathcal{Y}`$ is attached to exactly one group, in
the sense that $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{i}`$ for some $`i`$. In the context of
LLM reasoning, without loss of generality, we consider two groups for
brevity: $`\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ and $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$, corresponding
to regular-length CoT responses and extended responses (with low and
high inference costs), respectively. To conclude the formulation of
constrained RL with resource allocation constraints, we could in general
define the feasible set as a convex polytope,
$`\Phi_{\mathcal{G}}:=\{\pi:\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(x)}[\mathbbm{1}_{\{y\in\mathcal{G}_{i}\}}]\leq q_{i}\text{~for all $i$}\}`$,
that caps the total density mass of each group $`\mathcal{G}_{i}`$ by
$`q_{i}`$. In our setting, we only need to cap the total mass of
extended responses to optimize the inference efficiency, posing a
half-space
$`\Phi*{+}:=\{\pi:\mathbb{E}*{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(x)}[\mathbbm{1}_{\{y\in\mathcal{G}_{+}\}}]\leq q_{+}\}`$
for some $`q\_{+}>0`$.

Background. With the bandit setup, our setting draw a lot connection to
the online learning literature, especially online/bandit convex
optimization ([Hazan et al., 2016](#bib.bib26); [Slivkins et al.,
2019](#bib.bib60)), although we optimize a fixed function the training
data is however collected in an online fashion. In the sense of
distributing resources across groups, it is connected to for example
knapsack bandits ([Badanidiyuru et al., 2018](#bib.bib6)) and
statistical parity ([Zemel et al., 2013](#bib.bib77)), aka group
fairness. Although the definition of groups and optimization programs
could be different. This allocation optimization point of view allows us
to further extend our method to broader LLM applications. To the end of
policy optimization with respect to constraints, common techniques
include projection ([Zinkevich, 2003](#bib.bib82); [Flaxman et al.,
2004](#bib.bib20); [Bubeck et al., 2015](#bib.bib7); [Yang et al.,
2020](#bib.bib74)), Lyapunov-based ([Chow et al., 2018](#bib.bib13);
[Cayci et al., 2022](#bib.bib8)), or Lagrangian methods ([Ray et al.,
2019](#bib.bib57)).

Non-parametric space $`\Pi`$. In our case, our goal is to solve:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\max_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Pi_{\theta}}\mathcal{J}(\pi_{\theta})\quad\text{s.t.}~\pi_{\theta}\in\Phi_{+}\quad\text{where $\Pi_{\theta}$ is the parameterized policy space.}`$ |     | (1) |

Solving
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))
is however intractable due to the LLM parameterized policy space
$`\Pi_{\theta}`$. A common practice is alternating gradients between
reward maximization and constraint satisfaction. For example in
Lagrangian methods such as TRPO/PPO-Lagrangian ([Ray et al.,
2019](#bib.bib57)), one could do alternating update $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and
the Lagrangian multiplier. Another workaround is to first obtain a
solution $`\pi^{\star}`$ in the non-parametric policy space
$`\Pi:=\Delta(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})`$, aka tabular
representations, and project $`\pi^{\star}`$ onto the parameteric one
$`\Pi_{\theta}`$, as a technique used in many (constrained) RL
works ([Peters et al., 2010](#bib.bib53); [Montgomery and Levine,
2016](#bib.bib46); [Zhang et al., 2020](#bib.bib79)).

The advantage of working in the non-parametric space $`\Pi`$ is: solving
$`\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\mathcal{J}(\pi)`$ s.t. $`\pi\in\Phi_{+}`$ is easy, on
the conditions that (i) $`\mathcal{J}(\pi)`$ is concave in $`\pi`$ so
that it is a convex program, and (ii) sampling and evaluating the reward
function $`r(\cdot,\cdot)`$ and the cost indicator
$`\mathbbm{1}_{\{\cdot\}}`$ are cheap. The condition (i) is sometimes
true, for instances, bandit objective ([Slivkins et al.,
2019](#bib.bib60)); the LP formulation ([Manne, 1960](#bib.bib45);
[Denardo, 1970](#bib.bib17); [Nachum and Dai, 2020](#bib.bib47); [Nachum
et al., 2019](#bib.bib48)) of RL, and (relative) entropy regularized
RL ([Ziebart, 2010](#bib.bib80); [Haarnoja et al., 2017](#bib.bib24);
[Haarnoja et al., 2018](#bib.bib25)) are often concave in occupancy
measure $`\rho`$. However, in rare case condition (ii) holds, RL
works ([Haarnoja et al., 2018](#bib.bib25); [Peng et al.,
2019](#bib.bib52); [Zhang et al., 2020](#bib.bib79)) often resort to
value function approximation, making it is easy, for discrete action
space, to evaluate $`Q`$-values (or alternatively advantages) for all
actions for a specific state. It is then tractable to obtain closed-form
solution (optimal w.r.t. the value/advantage approximations) in $`\Pi`$.
Once an optimal policy $`\pi^{\star}`$ is found, one could then project
it onto $`\Pi_{\theta}`$ through (reverse) information projection
$`\theta=\argmin_{\theta}\mathbb{KL}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\theta})`$ (which
is often done approximately by taking gradient steps).

Stochastic optimization. With a LLM, it is obviously intractable to
sample and evaluate the reward function $`r(x,y)`$ for all
$`(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}`$, similarly for the cost
indicator $`\mathbbm{1}_{\{\cdot\}}`$. To avoid the training of
additional value models for LLMs ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib61); [Yu
et al., 2023](#bib.bib75)), which can create significant overhead in
terms of memory usage, implementation complexity, and training
stability, we consider a stochastic optimization. The stochastic
counterpart as described in
Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))
solves an approximate $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ using a manageable number of
samples rather than directly solving for the global optimum
$`\pi^{\star}`$, still, in the non-parametric space $`\Pi`$:

|     |                                                            |                                                                                                                                                        |                                                                                 |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\hat{\pi}^{\star}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})=`$ | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\argmax*{\pi\in\Pi}\hat{\mathcal{J}}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}):=\frac{1}{nm}\sum*{i}^{n}\sum*{j}^{m}[\pi(y*{ij} | x*{i})r(x*{i},y\_{ij})]`$                                                       |     | (2) |
|     |                                                            | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t.}~\pi\in\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}):=\{\pi:\textstyle\sum_{i}\sum*{j}[\pi(y*{ij}                                    | x*{i})\left(\mathbbm{1}*{\{y*{ij}\in\mathcal{G}*{+}\}}-q\_{+}\right)]\leq 0\}`$ |     |     |

where $`\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}`$ is a vector of $`n`$ sampled
prompts and $`\mathbf{Y}\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times m}`$ is a matrix of
responses, with $`m`$ responses for each of the $`n`$ prompts; we
explicitly write the empirical objective $`\hat{\mathcal{J}}`$ with the
conventional expected reward maximization for notational convenience,
though alternative objectives are not restricted.

Since the empirical
problem ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))
is a convex program with relative small sample size, it is now
manageable. Combing the aforementioned projection step, we could write
the program as a bi-level optimization:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |     |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\pi_{\theta}=\argmin_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\mathbb{KL}(\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\|\pi_{\theta})[x]\right]\quad\text{s.t.}~\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\in\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi\cap\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})}\hat{\mathcal{J}}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$ |     | (3) |

where $`\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})`$, and hence
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ is indirectly a function of $`\theta`$.

Practical update. For general bi-level optimization, iteratively solving
the upper and lower-level problems by alternatively fixing one while
optimizing the other could be expensive ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)). We’ve already setup a manageable inner problem,
making it easy to solve for example using convex solvers. One could
therefore do iterative gradient updates on the upper level while
directly solving the lower-level at each iteration:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\alpha\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\mu_{\mathbf{X}}}\left[\mathbb{KL}(\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\|\pi_{\theta})[x]\right]\quad\text{s.t.}~\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\in\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi\cap\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})}\hat{\mathcal{J}}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$ |     | (4) |

where $`\theta`$ and $`\theta^{\prime}`$ are the parameters of current
and next iteration, respectively; and the projection step is also done
as stochastic optimization with samples
$`(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$ of the current iteration.

Note that $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ is indirectly a function of $`\theta`$
through the samples $`(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$. The gradient
$`\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{KL}(\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\|\pi_{\theta})`$
hence requires differentiation through
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}`$, meaning
differentiate through an $`\argmax`$ operator, which can in principle be
achieved through implicit differentiation ([Amos and Kolter,
2017](#bib.bib3); [Lorraine et al., 2020](#bib.bib43)). However, to
avoid additional implementation and computation overhead, instead we use
the semi-gradient
$`{\nabla}_{\theta}\mathbb{KL}(\textsc{sg}\{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\}\|\pi_{\theta})`$,
where $`\textsc{sg}\{\cdot\}`$ is a stop gradient operator. This
stop-gradient trick is quite common in many ML applications ([Sutton,
2018](#bib.bib63); [Foerster et al., 2018](#bib.bib21); [Chen and He,
2021](#bib.bib10)), leading to the update:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\underbrace{\textstyle\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\alpha\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\mu_{\mathbf{X}}}\left[\mathbb{KL}(\textsc{sg}\{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\}\|\pi_{\theta})[x]\right]}_{\text{approximate projection / weighted SFT}}\quad\text{s.t.}~\underbrace{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\in\textstyle\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi\cap\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})}\hat{\mathcal{J}}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})}_{\text{optimization for weight}}`$ |     | (5) |

The semi-gradient
$`{\nabla}_{\theta}\mathbb{KL}(\textsc{sg}\{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\}\|\pi_{\theta})[x_{i}]=-\sum_{j}\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}(y_{ij}|x_{i})\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}|x_{i})`$
is a weighted SFT update (via $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$). This observation
creates an extremely simple update with negligible implementation
overhead.

Discussion. The update rule ended up aligning many iterative weighted
SFT algorithms, such as RAFT ([Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) and
RFT ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib49); [Touvron et al.,
2023](#bib.bib64)). In hindsight, our algorithm is motivated by the
observation that these extremely successful algorithms can be
interpreted as projecting empirical solutions onto a parametric space.
Consequently, it is reasonable to use the empirical estimate in
Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")),
as RAFT and RFT have demonstrated strong practical performance despite
the inherent bias introduced by the non-linearity of these estimations.
Since it is essentially generalizes SFT by re-weighting a sample pair
$`(x_{i},y_{ij})`$ by $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}(y_{ij}|x_{i})`$, at each
iteration based on the solution of an optimization problem
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$. We create a
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
outlines the corresponding components for some iterative SFT methods
from this optimization point-of-view.

|                      |                          |                                                                                                                                |                                                                                                                                      |                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| ALGO                 | loss $`\mathcal{L}`$     | reward $`r`$                                                                                                                   | feasible set $`\Phi`$                                                                                                                | weight/acceptance $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$                                                                                              |
| (Iterative) SFT      | $`\mathbb{XE}`$          | constant                                                                                                                       | $`\Pi`$                                                                                                                              | constant                                                                                                                             |
| RFT                  | weighted $`\mathbb{XE}`$ | binary                                                                                                                         | $`\Pi`$                                                                                                                              | $`\mathbbm{1}_{\{r(x,y)=1\}}`$                                                                                                       |
| RAFT (Best-of-$`N`$) | weighted $`\mathbb{XE}`$ | RM                                                                                                                             | $`\Pi`$                                                                                                                              | $`\mathbbm{1}_{\{r(x_{i},y)=\max_{j}r(x_{i},y_{ij})\}}`$                                                                             |
| Ours                 | weighted $`\mathbb{XE}`$ | Section [3](#S3 "3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization") | Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")) | Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")) |

Table 1: SFT methods from our optimization point-of-view.
$`\mathbb{XE}`$ denotes cross-entropy loss. RM stands for reward model,
binary reward indicates being correct or incorrect.
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ are (unnormalized) weights for the subsequent
$`\mathbb{XE}`$ update.

The optimization problems for RFT and RAFT are trivial, as they assign
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}(y|x)=1`$ to accepted responses and to the response
with the highest reward model score, respectively. Formulating these
methods as optimization does not offer much advantages. However, this
perspective provides flexibility for future work to extend our
framework, allowing for different feasible sets and weighting schemes
tailored to specific application needs.

## 3 Practical Implementation

Yet, as we are working in an algorithm-agnostic fashion, we are now
ready to select a specific RL algorithm, define its corresponding
objective $`\mathcal{J}`$, and specify an appropriate reward function
$`r`$.

Reward function. Since we are working on mathematical problem-solving, a
ground-truth reward could be obtained through string matching ([Cobbe
et al., 2021](#bib.bib14); [Hendrycks et al., 2021b](#bib.bib29)) of the
model’s solution against the ground truth solution, yielding a binary
reward function
$`r_{\mathrm{match}}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\{0,1\}`$ that
indicates correctness. On top of the binary reward, we define our reward
$`r_{\mathrm{\Delta}}`$ as the reward margin. To formally construct the
margin, we first define the expected reward of a set $`\mathcal{G}`$
such that
$`\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G}):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[r_{\mathrm{match}}(x,y)\mid y\in\mathcal{G}]`$.
We then define the reward margin $`r_{\mathrm{\Delta}}`$ as the reward
advantage of a group $`\mathcal{G}`$ against all other groups
$`\mathcal{Y}\setminus\mathcal{G}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r_{\Delta}(x,y\in\mathcal{G}):=\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G})-\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{Y}\setminus\mathcal{G})`$ |     | (6) |

In our case of two groups, we have
$`r_{\Delta}(x,y\in\mathcal{G}_{+})=\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G}_{+})-\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G}_{\circ})`$
and similarly for $`\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$. While $`r_{\Delta}`$ might
appear odd for not addressing the correctness of individual $`y`$, this
is handled subsequently.

RL objective. For the learning algorithm, our choice is Constraint
Generative Policy Optimization (CGPO) ([Xu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib72)),
which was originally designed for multi-objective constrained
optimization of LLMs. The choice is driven by implementation
considerations: CGPO’s modular constraint-handling design makes it
straightforward to incorporate additional constraints, such as the group
density constraint in our case. CGPO in a nutshell can be viewed as a
generalized Best-of-$`N`$ (BoN), though depending on the specific CGPO
settings. It operates by defining a feasible set $`\Xi`$ over the sample
space $`\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}`$, which are designed to capture
constraint adherence for, e.g. correctness, factuality, and safety ([Xu
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib72)). In short, $`(x,y)\notin\Xi`$ will be
rejected. In the context of math reasoning, the objective of CGPO can be
summarized as:

|     |                                                                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |                                                              |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[r(x,y)]`$ | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t.}~{\textstyle\sum\_{y}[\pi(y                                                                                                                                                                        | x)\mathbbm{1}_{\{y\in\Xi_{x}\}}]\geq 1}~\text{for all $x$}`$ |     | (7) |
|     |                                                                        | $`\displaystyle\text{where}~\Xi_{x}:=\{\underbrace{y:r_{\mathrm{match}}(x,y)=1}_{\text{correctness}}\}\cap\{\underbrace{y:\hat{\mathbb{KL}}(y;x,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\leq\mathbb{KL}_{\mathrm{max}}}_{\text{empirical KL}}\}`$ |                                                              |     |

This objective essentially optimizes reward over the feasible sets
$`\Xi_{x}`$ such that feasible response $`y`$ is correct and within an
KL range of $`\mathbb{KL}_{\mathrm{max}}`$, where the KL constraint is
measured using point estimate of the (forward) KL defined as
$`\hat{\mathbb{KL}}(y;x,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}):=\log\pi(y|x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)`$.

| prompt           | responses                               | $`r(x,y)`$             | $`r_{\Delta}(x,y)`$ | $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{1}=\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{cgpo}}`$^($`\dagger`$) | $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{2}=\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{cgpo}}`$^($`\ddagger`$) | $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}=\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$^($`\sharp`$) |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $`x_{1}`$ (easy) | $`y_{11},y_{12}\in\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ | $`\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ |

1&1\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ | 0 |  $`\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |  $`\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&1\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |  $`\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&0\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |
|  | $`y*{13},y*{14}\in\mathcal{G}_{+}`$ |  | 0 |  |  |  |
| $`x_{2}`$ (hard) | $`y*{21},y*{22}\in\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ |  $`\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
1&1\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ | -0.5 |  $`\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&0\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |  $`\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |  $`\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\\
\end{pmatrix}`$ |
|  | $`y_{23},y*{24}\in\mathcal{G}*{+}`$ | | 0.5 | | | |

- $`\dagger`$
  CGPO case 1: for $`x_{2}`$ (hard), $`y_{21}\in\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ is
  accepted though $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$ has greater expected return
  $`\bar{r}(x_{2},\mathcal{G}_{+})`$.
- $`\ddagger`$
  CGPO case 2: $`y_{14}`$ and $`y_{23}`$ are accepted, exceeding the
  density budget of $`q_{+}=0.5`$.
- $`\sharp`$
  Ours: $`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ accepts $`y_{11}`$ and
  $`y_{23}`$ so that margin is maximized
  ($`r_{\Delta}(x_{2},y_{23})=0.5`$), and density cap $`q_{+}`$ holds.

Table 2: A concrete example of $`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ compared
to
$`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{cgpo}}`$-Eq. ([7](#S3.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))-
with tie broken randomly, resulting in potentially non-unique
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$. This table shows several such
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ solutions but not all. KL constraint is omitted
for brevity. Given the rewards defined below, we have
$`\bar{r}(x_{1},\mathcal{G}_{\circ})=\bar{r}(x_{1},\mathcal{G}_{+})=\bar{r}(x_{2},\mathcal{G}_{+})=1`$
and $`\bar{r}(x_{2},\mathcal{G}_{\circ})=0.5`$. Suppose the density
constraint $`q_{+}=0.5`$, allowing at most $`50`$% of accepted responses
are extended $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{+}`$. For a solution matrix
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$, $`1`$ and $`0`$ represent accepted and rejected
response, respectively.

Resulted update (IBPO). Recap our update was defined as
$`\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\alpha\nabla_{\theta}{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\mu_{\mathbf{X}}}\left[\mathbb{KL}(\textsc{sg}\{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\}\|\pi_{\theta})[x]\right]`$
subject to
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\in\argmax_{\pi\in\Pi\cap\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})}\hat{\mathcal{J}}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$,
in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Algorithm Design ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
And we’ve now defined the RL objective $`\mathcal{J}`$ and the margin
reward function $`r_{\Delta}`$. We are now ready to put everything
together:

|     |                                                                        |                                                                                                                                                                              |                                                                                                                                                          |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}}\in`$ | $`\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\argmax*{\pi}\textstyle\hat{\mathcal{J}}*{\Delta}(\pi;\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta}):=\frac{1}{nm}\sum_{i}^{n}\sum*{j}^{m}[\pi(y*{ij} | x*{i})r*{\Delta}(x*{i},y*{ij})]`$                                                                                                                        |     | (8) |
|     |                                                                        | $`\displaystyle\underbrace{\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\text{s.t.}~\pi\in\Pi\cap\hat{\Phi}_{+}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})\text{~and~}\textstyle\sum\_{y}[\pi(y             | x)\mathbbm{1}_{\{y\in\Xi_{x}\}}]\geq 1~\text{for all $x\in\mathbf{X}$}}_{\text{shorthanded as $\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}$ (inference under budget)}}`$ |     |     |

In addition, as CGPO is a generalization of BoN (with tie breaking
randomly), $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ will be a pure strategy instead of
stochastic one, meaning at most one $`y`$ will be accepted for each
$`x`$, for subsequent projection (SFT).

Intuition. Behind this update our intuition can be interpreted as: for a
mini-batch $`(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}_{\theta})`$, $`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$
aims to maximize the expected margin, while staying within the density
constraints specified feasible region $`\hat{\Phi}_{+}`$; and in
addition, only assign positive weight to responses $`y\in\Xi_{x}`$,
meaning $`y`$ is both correct and within KL range.

Or verbally, if a prompt $`x`$ is difficult, the margin of extended
responses
$`r_{\Delta}(x,y\in\mathcal{G}_{+})=\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G}_{+})-\bar{r}_{\pi}(x,\mathcal{G}_{\circ})`$
is likely to be large for $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{+}`$. Therefore
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ will more likely to assign positive weight to an
extended response $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{+}`$ so that the objective receive
more margin reward. On the other hand, if a query $`x`$ is simple,
$`r_{\Delta}(x,y\in\mathcal{G}_{+})`$ is likely to be small. Hence
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}`$ will possibly assign positive weight to regular
responses $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$, so that one could save some
density budget for harder queries. A concrete example is given in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

Reward models. Note that the original CGPO implementation has reward
models for BoN ranking. We however intentionally excludes reward models,
in our $`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ formulation as shown in
Eq. ([8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")),
to highlight our methodological contributions, by decoupling reward
modeling efforts. Nonetheless, using reward models remains possible. To
avoid introducing additional notation, we elaborate verbally:
$`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ essentially selects either group
$`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$ or $`\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ for a query $`x`$. Within
a group $`\mathcal{G}`$, all responses receive the same reward
$`r_{\Delta}(x,\mathcal{G})`$, leaving it possible to further rank
responses within each group using reward models.

Implementation & solvers. A pseudo-code of our IBPO with
$`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ is listed in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
The essential change is to replace the constrained reward ranking
$`\textsc{opt}_{\textsc{cgpo}}`$ with a general optimization problem, in
our case the margin maximization under budget denoted as
$`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$. The $`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$
problem is a (integer) linear programming problem that could be solved
by off-the-shelf solvers, such as CPLEX ([Cplex, 2009](#bib.bib15)),
Gurobi ([Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2024](#bib.bib23)) or
SciPy ([Virtanen et al., 2020](#bib.bib66)), which is our choice.

$`m`$, init policy $`\pi_{0}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$, num of iters $`T`$,
budgets $`q_{+}`$

$`\mathbf{X}^{n}\sim\mu_{\mathbb{D}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{Y}^{n\times m}_{\theta}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{X})`$

3:   evaluate correctness and empirical KL:
$`\mathbf{R}^{n\times m}_{\mathrm{match}}=r_{\mathrm{match}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})`$
and
$`\hat{\mathbf{KL}}^{n\times m}=\hat{\mathbb{KL}}(\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{X},\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})`$

5:    solve Best-of-$`N`$:

as defined in

as defined in
Eq. ([8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")),
using solver

Figure 2: Prompt templates. For $`\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$, we use the SCoT
prompt without including an additional \[condition description\] and
generate a standard SCoT response. For $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$, we simply
insert the corresponding condition into the \[condition description\]
placeholder to create a new prompt. In the case of SV, the SV condition
is integrated into the prompt, and the model is asked to perform
repeated trials to reach a consensus. The ASV prompt instructs the model
to output either a voting response (case 1) or a non-voting response
(case 2), with the decision made by the model itself.

## 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$ & Training Pipelines

Yet we work on abstract groups $`\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ and
$`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$. In this section, we present the details of our
constructions of extended length responses, i.e. the extended group
$`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$. However developing long reasoning models is beyond
the scope of this work, as our focus is on the constrained optimization
of LLMs. Our constructions are for demonstrative purpose only. Due to
the intricate details involved in prompts, datasets, and training
pipelines, this section may appear somewhat dense. To make it more
approachable, we have structured our writing in a way that readers can,
if they wish, focus on the broader ideas without delving deeply into the
specifics of constructions. A TL;DR version of this section is provided
below.

TL;DR. We construct two types of illustrative extended responses:
Sequential Voting (SV) and Adaptive Sequential Voting (ASV).
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
visually explains how these constructions are implemented. The goal of
the SV is to establish a baseline that generates only responses in
$`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$, thereby serving as an uni-modal comparator. SV
scales roughly as well as vanilla majority voting (MV), aka
self-consistency ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib68)). In contrast, ASV
outputs a mixture of responses of $`y\in\mathcal{G}_{\circ}`$ and
$`y\in\mathcal{G}_{+}`$. This allows the model to adaptively decide
which type of response to produce based on the query. The goal of ASV is
to further enable IBPO optimization, as IBPO implicitly assumes the
model generates both regular and extended-length responses. In
Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
we show that ASV optimized by IBPO, achieves better allocation of the
inference budget.

### 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote

Acronyms. For clarity, we explicitly define key terms to hopefully
resolve any potential ambiguities. Response: A response refers to a
sequence generated until a terminal token is encountered. For precision,
we sometimes refer to these as voting responses or SCoT responses, as
illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
after introducing our sequential voting baselines. Trial: A trial
denotes a solution instance, which is demarcated by the special tokens
\[TRIAL\] … \[/TRIAL\], as shown in the voting response example in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
While a voting response contains multiple trials, a SCoT response or a
non-voting response contains exactly one trial, as also depicted in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

For the description of training and testing details, we use LLaMA and
LLaMA-b to denote the instruction-tuned and base versions of the LLaMA
3.1 8B models ([Dubey et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), respectively. MATH
refers specifically to the training split of the Hendrycks MATH
dataset ([Hendrycks et al., 2021b](#bib.bib29)), while the 500-sample
subset of the testing split is referred to as MATH500 ([Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib41)). SDPO stands for step-DPO ([Lai et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38)) dataset, a curated step-annotated dataset from which
we retain only the prompts and positive responses (ground truth
solutions), excluding any step signals (see
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
for details). It is important to note that while we leverage their
curated dataset, the original SDPO method is not relevant to this work.
The SDPO dataset was chosen because its ground truth responses follow
the SCoT format of LLaMA responses, making it convenient to run
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mixed with LLaMA samples.

Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Performance of Naiv̈e Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),

Construction details. To be more specific, the naïve sequential voting
baselines, as the “expensive” group $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$, have increased
inference costs by simply sequentially output multiple trials and find
the sequential majority vote until stop condition met. In particular,
the early-stopping sequential voting (SV) baseline is created to show
that such naïve baseline could achieve performance gain, on par with
vanilla majority voting (MV). The adaptive sequential voting (ASV)
allows model to output both SCoT response $`y_{\circ}`$ and sequential
voting response $`y_{+}`$, allowing us to further conduct the budget
controll experiments in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

- •
  Early Stopping Sequential Vote (SV): For a single response, model are
  allowed to output at most 8 trials, and conclude with majority of
  trials. In addition to the terminal condition of maximum 8 trials,
  model will early stop if an answer appears 3 times and this answer
  will be considered as the majority answer.
- •
  Adaptive Sequential Vote (ASV): Model is allowed to choose either vote
  (case 1, i.e. $`y_{+}`$) or not (case 2, i.e. $`y_{\circ}`$). This
  baseline is created to further allow model-driven resource allocation.
  We later, in
  Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
  show that one could optimize the ability of resource allocation with
  our IBPO.

Dataset. We define our construction of dataset as a product of a problem
set $`\mathbb{Q}`$, format template of question $`\mathcal{T}_{q}`$ and
answer $`\mathcal{T}_{a}`$, and a response set $`\mathbb{A}`$, subjected
to some filtration $`\mathcal{F}`$. Formally, a dataset $`\mathbb{D}`$
is defined as:
$`\mathbb{D}:=(\mathcal{F}\circ\mathcal{T}_{q}\circ\mathcal{T}_{a})(\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{A})`$,
where $`\mathcal{F}`$ removes undesired question-answer pairs, such as
incorrect responses when $`\mathbb{A}`$ are model generated; The
templates $`\mathcal{T}_{q}`$ and $`\mathcal{T}_{a}`$ collectively
transform each question-answer pair into a specific text format, as
shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization");
Slightly abusing the notation, the Cartesian product
$`\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{A}`$ is used to pair each response with its
corresponding question, defined as:
$`\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{A}:={\{(q_{i},a_{ij}):\forall i,j\}}`$.

Specifically, we summarize the datasets used in subsequent sections in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
For instance, for SV training, we construct $`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{sv}}`$
with question set $`\mathbb{Q}_{\textsc{math}}`$ from [Hendrycks et al.
(2021b)](#bib.bib29) and LLaMA generated responses
$`\mathbb{A}^{\textsc{sample}}_{\textsc{math}}`$ using the SV templates
defined in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
subjected to data selection described in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

is the summary of our IBPO training, using dataset
$`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{rl}}`$ as constructed in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
and initialized from ASV models from experiment 2.2. Further details of
each training can be found in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
and [E](#A5 "Appendix E Hyperparameters ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

### 4.2 Performance of Naiv̈e Sequential Vote

We start by evaluating the performance of SV compared to vanilla MV,
following the setup of Exp. 1.1 in
Table [6](#S4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
This toy experiment is designed to demonstrate: (i) SV scales
approximately as well as MV, thereby qualifying it as an example of
$`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$; and (ii) measuring performance based on the number
of responses is inadequate, therefore we later measure performance
relative to the number of tokens/trials in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

Metrics. The metrics we use are pass@$`k`$ and majority@$`k`$, both of
which are widely used in the literature ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021b](#bib.bib29); [Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib68)). We occasionally
refer to pass rate as pass@$`1`$. In both metrics, $`k`$ specifically
denotes the number of responses, regardless of the number of trials per
response. Since our voting methods may involve multiple trials, we may
use the average number of trials (as illustrated in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))
on the x-axis for cost-aware comparisons. In addition, we evaluate
“performance-cost” efficiency by comparing each method’s scaling
efficiency to that of MV, following the comparison in [Snell et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib62).

As shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
SV exhibits significant improvements—nearly 10%—in terms of
majority@$`k`$ when performance is measured by the number of responses.
However, this improvement is misleading since each SV response
effectively consists of multiple SCoT responses. Therefore, measuring
performance with taking length into consideration provides a more
reasonable assessment. As demonstrated in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
SV’s scaling performance aligns with that of vanilla MV, supporting its
role as a suitable construction example for $`\mathcal{G}_{+}`$.

## 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ $`\textsc{OPT}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$

### 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))

“Baselines”. To put SV/ASV in comparison with other baselines in
literature, we gather several baselines from the self-correction
literature as essentially these methods increase inference length,
though not extensively as [Jaech et al. (2024)](#bib.bib33). The results
in
Table [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
are mainly gathered from [Qu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib55); [Kumar et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib37). The self-correction baselines often admit a
multi-turn structure, similarly to the multi-trial construction of SV.
We therefore include a column of inference cost measured by number of
turns/trials for a rough comparison. The SFT comparators we include are
(reproduced) Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)),
STaR ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib76)), S³C ([Yan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib73)), SFT-RI and SFT-SCoRe, where SFT-RI and SFT-SCoRe are
SFT comparators implemented in Recursive Introspection (RI) ([Qu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)) and SCoRe ([Kumar et al., 2024](#bib.bib37))
respectively.

ASV experiments. SV-SFT follows our training pipeline of Exp 1.2 in
Table [6](#S4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
and is an voting only baseline. ASV-SFT-$`\alpha`$ follows our Exp 2.1
setup and is an adpative baseline, meaning model decide whether to vote
or not for a problem. We report ASV-SFT-$`1`$ only as it is empirically
the best adaptive baseline although still fall short in terms of
efficiency. Our ASV-IuB-$`q_{+}`$ experiments, all initialized from
ASV-SFT-$`1`$, are our adaptive models, optimized by IBPO with
$`\textsc{opt}_{\mathrm{IuB}}`$ as lower level optimization, e.g.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").

Observations. We would like to first emphasize that the comparison in
Table [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
is not intended to demonstrate that SV outperforms SFT-based
self-correction or that our ASV-IuB surpasses RL-based self-corrections.
These efforts are orthogonal, as our focus is on constrained
optimization. As observed, our SFT constructions—SV-SFT and ASV-SFT-1
achieve a clear improvement in pass@$`1`$ with high inference costs
($`5+`$ times the number of trials). The ASV-IuB-$`q_{+}`$ formulation,
particularly with $`q_{+}=\{50\%,75\%\}`$, shows significant improvement
while reducing costs by $`4.14\%`$ at $`2.16\times`$ and $`5.74\%`$ at
$`4.32\times`$. This performance is on par with SCoRe, a
state-of-the-art RL-based self-correction method. Note that the
performance of ASV-IuB-$`q_{+}`$ is reported using the best checkpoints.
Results from the last checkpoint are shown in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
Additionally, training curves are presented in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Further Discussions ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
which shows consistent improvements. As a somewhat tangential yet
potentially intriguing observation, it is evident that prompting-based
and SFT-based methods struggle with both absolute improvement
(Table [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))
and efficiency
(Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")),
supporting the conjecture that SFT alone does not enable self-correction
capabilities ([Huang et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Kumar et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)). This observation is also partially supported by
concurrent work ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), which suggests
that such self-correction behavior emerges automatically during RL
rather than manually created by prompting or SFT.

### 5.2 Efficiency, Constraint Following & Budget Allocation

Table [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Construction of Sequential Vote ‣ 4 Acronyms, Naïve Construction 𝒢_+ & Training Pipelines ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
demonstrates that our ASV-IuB-$`q+`$ models can achieve performance
comparable to RL-based self-correction models simply through inference
allocation management. In this subsection, we elaborate on our
discussion of (i) performance-budget efficiency, (ii) constraint
satisfaction, and (iii) inference budget allocation.

Performance-budget efficiency. In
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
we visually assess the performance-budget efficiency, compared to a
hypothetical efficiency boundary. This boundary is an interpolation
between OSS LLaMA model and SV-SFT. It is reasonable to see it as a
hypothetical boundary for two reasons: (i) OSS and SV-SFT are two
extremes of ASV-IuB-$`q_{+}`$, corresponding to the cases of $`q*{+}=0`$
and $`q*{+}=1`$ respectively; and (ii) this interpolation achieves an
increase comparable to MV, if not slightly better. The SFT version of
ASV is generally much worse than the boundary, as SFT alone does not
optimize resource allocation as a mathematical objective. For
ASV-IuB-$`q*{+}`$ optimized by IBPO, we report both the last and best
checkpoint results in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
and
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
respectively. Our formulation achieves, in general, better
performance-budget efficiency, except $`q*{+}=75\%`$ in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
We will extend our discussion on this unsuccessful case in subsequent
paragraphs.

Constraint satisfaction. We then evaluate how effectively the
constraints are enforced. In
Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
the budget constraints are successfully maintained during training for
$`q_{+}=\{25\%,50\%,75\%\}`$. Due to distribution shifts, exact
adherence to these constraints is not expected on the test set.
Nevertheless,
Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
demonstrates that constraints are still upheld at the end of training
for $`q\_{+}=\{25\%,50\%\}`$, and the ratio of voting responses follows
the order $`75\%\succ 50\%\succ 25\%`$.
(Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
illustrates that our model meets the budget constraints for the set of
correct responses. The constraints also hold for all responses, see
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Further Discussions ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").)

Difficulty-aware allocation. While we have demonstrated improved
efficiency and adherence to constraints, we would like to validate the
underlying intuition of our design: that more challenging problems may
require longer reasoning steps, whereas simpler problems can be resolved
with just SCoT responses. Ideally, the model should allocate more voting
responses to problems with higher difficulty levels. To this end, we use
the difficulty levels from the metadata of Hendrycks MATH and plot the
ratio of voting responses for each difficulty level.
Figure [14](#S5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
illustrates that for both $`q_{+}=\{25\%,50\%\}`$, more challenging
problems, such as those at levels 4 and 5, receive a higher allocation
of budgets. This allocation pattern is particularly evident for the case
of $`q\_{+}=25\%`$, where only $`2\%`$ of level 1 problems receive voting
responses.

Discussion on the unsuccessful case. There is one observed unsuccessful
case in
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"):
the last checkpoint of ASV-IuB-$`75\%`$, which falls on the hypothetical
boundary rather than above it. This outcome is arguably expected, as
observed in
Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1 Absolute Improvement (Table ) ‣ 5 Evaluation of IBPO w/ "OPT"\_IuB ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
where ASV-IuB-$`75\%`$ outputs almost exclusively voting responses at
the end of training. As a result, this model is not adaptively
allocating resources, and thus no improvement in efficiency is
anticipated. This unsuccessful case is hence caused by the distribution
shift between the training set and the testing set. It is possible that
scaling the training set—given that our training set
$`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{rl}}`$ contains approximately $`10,000`$ prompts,
which is relatively small—will make the testing set more likely to be
in-distribution and thereby alleviate the distribution shift issue.

## 6 Conclusion & Discussions

We derived a constrained policy optimization framework, IBPO, from an
optimization perspective, resulting in a simple weighted SFT update that
resembles successful iterative SFT algorithms such as RFT and RAFT. In
each iteration, the optimal weight is determined by solving an (integer)
linear program. The practical implementation of IBPO is build on top of
CGPO, and is evaluated on a math reasoning task with inference budget
constraints. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our framework
enables the model to adhere to constraints and dynamically allocate the
inference budget.

Batch optimization. Since we solve an optimization problem per iteration
(i.e. per mini-batch), limited computational resources can result in
smaller sample sizes for the inner optimization problem, leading to
larger variance. This issue can be mitigated through “sample
accumulation”, accumulating samples across multiple consecutive steps,
similar to gradient accumulation practice in LLMs. A pseudo-code for
sample accumulation can be found in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C MILP Solving ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
In addition, though integer linear programming is NP-hard ([Vazirani,
1997](#bib.bib65)), the number of variables in our batch-level
optimization is typically small, resulting in minimal computational
overhead. Refer to the wall-time plot for the SciPy solver in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C MILP Solving ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization")
for further details.

Controlled setting. We keep our experiment setting minimal: we do not
use reward models; we use only an 8B model to generate any set of
sampled responses, $`\mathbb{A}^{\textsc{sample}}`$. Our RL training
set, $`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{rl}}`$, contains only 10k prompts, leaving
the setting quite controlled and providing room for improvement through
engineering efforts.

Limitations. Our work is limited in its choice of RL algorithms and
applications. While it should be straightforward to apply our framework
to different RL frameworks, additional effort is required to derive an
optimization problem for different application tasks. Future work may
include extending our constrained policy optimization framework to a
broader range of LLM applications or scaling up our experiments.

Broader applications. Although our framework has only been evaluated
with inference budget allocation, the resource allocation problem has
far-reaching implications within the ML community. As a result, our
framework can be potentially extended to further LLM applications. For
example, a promising application is statistical parity ([Zemel et al.,
2013](#bib.bib77)), aka group fairness. In this context, one could
consider attributing responses to their respective social groups, and
cap the density of responses that correspond to socially privileged
groups, to encourage more inclusive and equitable responses across
different demographics. Another potential application is the balanced
activation of mixture of experts ([Jacobs et al., 1991](#bib.bib32);
[Shazeer et al., 2017](#bib.bib58); [Lepikhin et al.,
2020](#bib.bib39)), which is sometimes achieved by adding an auxiliary
loss ([Wei et al., 2024](#bib.bib70)). Alternatively, this balance can
be possibly achieved by enforcing a minimal total activation density for
each expert. This may help to prevent over-reliance on a subset of
experts, and hence enhancing the overall robustness and efficiency. We
leave the exploration of broader applications and their implementations
as future directions.

## Appendix B Batch Accumulation

This is a batch accumulation implementation of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
For brevity, we use $`\textsc{opt}_{\textsc{iub}}`$ as an example. One
could increase the optimization problem size of $`n\times m`$ to
$`(n\cdot k_{b})\times(m\cdot k_{r})`$ using
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix B Batch Accumulation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
where superscripts indicate matrix shape, left subscripts denote
accumulation indices (distinguishing them from element indices).

0:  prompt set $`\mathbb{D}`$, batch size $`n`$, number of responses
$`m`$, init policy $`\pi_{0}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$, num of iters $`T`$,
budgets $`q_{+}`$

1:  for $`t=1,\ldots,T`$ do

2:   for $`i=1,\ldots,k_{b}`$ do

3:    prompt sampling:
$`\prescript{}{i}{\mathbf{X}}^{n}\sim\mu_{\mathbb{D}}`$

4:    for $`j=1,\ldots,k_{r}`$ do

5:     response generation:
$`\prescript{}{ij}{\mathbf{Y}}^{n\times m}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\prescript{}{i}{\mathbf{X}})`$

6:    end for

7:   end for

8:   prompt accumulation:
$`\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(n\cdot k_{b})}=[\prescript{}{1}{\mathbf{X}},\prescript{}{2}{\mathbf{X}},\cdots,\prescript{}{k_{b}}{\mathbf{X}}]`$

9:   response accumulation:
$`\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}^{(n\cdot k_{b})\times(m\cdot k_{r})}=[\prescript{}{11}{\mathbf{Y}},\prescript{}{12}{\mathbf{Y}},\cdots,\prescript{}{1k_{r}}{\mathbf{Y}};\cdots;\prescript{}{k_{b}1}{\mathbf{Y}},\prescript{}{k_{b}2}{\mathbf{Y}},\cdots,\prescript{}{k_{b}k_{r}}{\mathbf{Y}}]`$

10:   evaluate correctness and empirical KL:
$`\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{match}}=r_{\mathrm{match}}(\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\mathbf{Y}})`$
and
$`\hat{\mathbf{KL}}=\hat{\mathbb{KL}}(\tilde{\mathbf{Y}};\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})`$

11:   margin maximization:
$`\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}}\in\textsc{opt}_{\textsc{iub}}(\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\mathbf{Y}},\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{match}},\hat{\mathbf{KL}},q_{+})`$
as defined in
Eq. ([8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 3 Practical Implementation ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"))

12:   gradient update: with
$`-\sum_{i=1}^{n\cdot k_{b}}\sum_{j=1}^{m\cdot k_{r}}{\hat{\pi}^{\star}_{\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}}(y_{ij}|x_{i})}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}|x_{i})\big|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}`$

13:  end for

Algorithm 2 IBPO with Sample Accumulation

## Appendix C MILP Solving

We use SciPy MILP solver, available
[here](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.milp.html),
to solve our in-batch integer linear programming optimizations. A
Pythonic pseudo code is available in Figure . And the wall-time consumed
could be found in
Figure [15](#A3.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ Appendix C MILP Solving ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
In general, the problem size is small, so the computational overhead is
negligible.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 import numpy as np

2 from scipy.optimize import milp, LinearConstraint, Bounds

3

4 def solve_iub(acceptance, is_vote, budget):

5 """ solves a Inference under Budget (IuB) problem.

6 parameters:

7 - acceptance: an n x m array where each element is 1 if accepted, 0
otherwise.

8 - is_vote: an n x m array indicating whether response is voting (1)
or non-voting (0).

9 - budget: the fractional budget (q+) constraint for the problem. """

10 n, m = acceptance.shape

11 \# calculate pass rates for vote-based and non-vote-based responses

12 vote_pass_rate = np.mean(acceptance \* is_vote, axis=1,
keepdims=True)

13 sample_pass_rate = np.mean(acceptance \* (1 - is_vote), axis=1,
keepdims=True)

14 margin = vote_pass_rate - sample_pass_rate \# (n, 1)

15 \# flattern acceptance and vote indicator, tile the margin

16 acceptance = np.reshape(acceptance, -1) \# (n x m, )

17 is_vote = np.reshape(is_vote, -1) \# (n x m, )

18 margin = np.reshape(np.tile(margin, \[1, m\]), -1) \# (n x m, )

19

20 \# define the objective function coefficients

21 c = -1 \* margin \* is_vote + margin \* (1 - is_vote)

22 \# acceptance constraints: ensure each prompt meets acceptance
criteria

23 A_acceptance = np.eye(len(acceptance))

24 b_acceptance = acceptance

25 \# one response per problem constraint (BoN)

26 A_problem = np.zeros((n, n \* m))

27 for i in range(n):

28 A_problem\[i, i \* m:(i + 1) \* m\] = 1

29 b_problem = np.ones(n)

30 \# voting responses budget constraint

31 A_vote_budget = np.where(is_vote == 1, 1, 0).reshape(1, -1)

32 vote_budget = np.round(budget \* len(acceptance))

33

34 \# combine all constraints into a single matrix

35 A = np.vstack(\[A_acceptance, A_problem, A_vote_budget\])

36 b_lower = -np.inf \* np.ones(A.shape\[0\]) \# lower bounds for
constraints

37 b_upper = np.hstack(\[b_acceptance, b_problem, vote_budget\]) \#
upper bounds

38 \# solve the MILP problem using the defined objective and constraints

39 result = milp(c, integrality=np.ones(len(c)), bounds=Bounds(0, 1),

40 constraints=LinearConstraint(A, b_lower, b_upper))

41 return result

Listing 1: Pythonic code snippet for solving IuB with SciPy: Note that
this is for demonstration purposes, and error-free execution is not
guaranteed, due to omitted corner cases.

![Refer to caption](2501.17974v2/figures/wall_time.png)

## Appendix D Data Construction

We elaborate on the details of $`\mathbb{Q}_{\textsc{sdpo}}`$,
$`\mathbb{A}_{\textsc{sdpo}}^{\textsc{golden}}`$,
$`\mathbb{Q}_{\textsc{math}}`$,
$`\mathbb{A}_{\textsc{math}}^{\textsc{sample}}`$, and the filteration
function $`\mathcal{F}`$.

SDPO dataset. [Lai et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38) create a dataset (see
their Section 3.2) contains 10,795 step-wise preference pairs, where the
winning response is a correct solution, the losing response is incorrect
starting from certain step. For our purpose of SFT and RL training, we
do not need losing responses, hence we create
$`\mathbb{A}_{\textsc{sdpo}}^{\textsc{golden}}`$ with only wining
(correct) responses. The step-formatted response (see an example below)
is the reason we choose the dataset from [Lai et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib38), as it adhere the SCoT format of LLaMA models.
Therefore, one do not need to worry about potential format changes.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

SV dataset for MATH. We also created datasets,
$`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{sv}}`$ and $`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{asv1}}`$, for SFT
so that a model could follow the SV instructions. We take
$`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{sv}}`$ as an example and
$`\mathbb{D}_{\textsc{asv1}}`$ could be created similarly. To do so, we
first generate $`32`$ responses per prompt for the entire MATH training
split with a temperature of $`1.2`$ and top-p of $`0.9`$. We then apply
our SV templates $`\mathcal{T}_{q}`$ and $`\mathcal{T}_{a}`$ to create
corresponding SV question and answer pairs. The procedure of creating a
SV response is given by
Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
While we have include an example of SV responses in
Figure [16](#A4.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization"),
we make it more concrete the SV response template below,

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 16: SV response templates. Left: suppose a consensus is found at
$`k`$-th answer; Right: no consensus found. Note the subscript $`i`$ of
$`A_{i}`$ only denotes index of answer, $`A_{i}`$ and $`A_{j}`$ could
still have same final answer for $`i\neq j`$.

0:  template $`\mathcal{T}_{q}`$, $`\mathcal{T}_{a}`$, a problem $`Q`$,
a set of shuffled responses $`\{A_{i}:i=1,2,\cdots,K\}`$

1:  create prompt: $`\mathcal{T}_{q}(Q)`$ replace problem placeholder
with $`Q`$

2:  responses = \[\]; final_answer = \[INVALID_ANSWER\]; found = False

3:  for $`i=1,2,\cdots,K`$ do

4:   responses.append($`A_{i}`$)

5:   majority = find_majority(responses)

6:   majority_count = count_majority(responses, majority)

7:   if majority_count == 3 then

8:    found = True; final_answer = majority; break

9:   end if

10:  end for

11:  if found == False and responses contain correct solution then

12:   final_answer = random pick a correct solution

13:  end if

14:  create SV response:
$`\mathcal{T}_{a}(\text{responses, final\_answer})`$

Algorithm 3 Creating SV Response for SFT .

We then apply some filtration $`\mathcal{F}`$ to the created dataset. We
remove any SV responses where the final answers are incorrect. From the
remaining set, we sub-sample 500 question-response pairs. These pairs
are selected from problems that have between 4 and 8 distinct answers
out of 32 samples, ensuring that we construct sequential responses with
a diverse trials. The distribution of trial counts and distinct answer
counts are shown in
Figure [19](#A4.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ Appendix D Data Construction ‣ Think Smarter not Harder: Adaptive Reasoning with Inference Aware Optimization").
It can be observed that the filtered data is generally diversely
distributed.
